newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada offers C$425 mln for infrastructure plan.
newsitem.headline: Canada offers C$425 mln for infrastructure plan.

text.p: The Canadian government offered on Tuesday to put up a further C$425 million to extend the country's infrastructure program in 1997 and create up to 20,000 jobs.
The government's offer would add to the C$175 million budgeted under the existing program, begun soon after the Liberals came to power in 1993.

When combined with contributions of provinces and local governments, the federal offer could create infrastructure investments of about C$1.8 billion across Canada in 1997, a government statement said.

"Our proposal could support about 2,500 new projects across the country and create between 15,000 and 20,000 jobs in the construction sector and construction-related industries," Treasury Board President Marcel Masse said.
"Since last summer, our (provincial and municipal) partners have shown interest in the extension of the infrastructure program but they also talked about the tight fiscal situation that we all face."
Some provinces said previously they were not interested in putting up their third of the cost, and it was unclear how many would agree to this proposal.
Treasury Board spokesman Daniel Lavoie told Reuters that one province, which he did not identify, had so far agreed. Masse made the offer in a December 27 letter.

Masse said in his statement that the federal offer "accounts for this reality" of fiscal constraint. Asked to explain, Lavoie said it was scaled back from the original three-year program of C$2 billion a year.

Masse's letter said the extension of the program should "aim at job-creation impacts in 1997," leading the Globe and Mail newspaper to suggest the government was trying to sweeten voters for a general election expected this year.
